source.title: Compression Precedes, Content Decides: Emergent Misalignment in Reward Models

record.tranche_reason: Extends emergent-misalignment research to reward models and reports its own results, but measures reward-model preference inversion and related representations rather than the refusal or bypass behaviors in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmful-preference rates for reward models, preference likelihoods for language models, and representation angles. These are related findings, but they do not measure the claim versions' specified refusal rates, per-token KL, bypass success, safety-carrying parameters, or deepened safety. The generation-level result is stated in prose as a range for SFT and a total for DPO without enough detail to assign the results to specific model and training arms.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. It fine-tunes Bradley–Terry reward models and their instruct backbones on harmful-preference pairs. It then measures reward-model preference P(c>r), language-model likelihood preference P(m>0), activation angles, and emergent misalignment on Betley et al.'s open-ended questions. It never measures chat-model compliance with harmful user requests, per-token KL against a base model, prefill, suffix or decoding bypass, safety-carrying parameters, or a deepening method. It does not cite either original source. T3 is wrong because the results are not on the claim, so the tranche is T6, related work only.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the same data inverts the reward model more completely than its language-model backbone. Also add that the inversion is attributed to a content-specific rotation of harmful representations toward the scalar head, which occurs only in harmful fine-tunes.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes reward models on harmful-versus-sound preference pairs and evaluates reward preferences and activation geometry; it does not reproduce a chat-model refusal test, per-token KL measurement, or bypass intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The harmful-preference outcome varies by model, training domain, and evaluation set: RM-Qwen financial fine-tuning reaches 0.510 on the open-ended evaluation while RM-Llama reaches 0.369; the paper also reports different residual control preferences under LoRA and full fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA fine-tuning on 1,000 harmful-preference pairs from one domain raises reward models' harmful preference from 0.000 to 0.876–0.976 on 799 held-out pairs. The politeness control reaches 0.073–0.095 under LoRA and 0.194 under full fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow harmful-preference fine-tuning inverts reward-model preferences across held-out domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Inversion transfers more weakly to open-ended Betley question pairs: 0.169–0.369 for RM-Llama and 0.237–0.510 for RM-Qwen. The control stays near 0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-model harm preference partially transfers to open-ended questions, with strength depending on model and training domain.

fits_no_version.finding: The instruct backbones trained on the same pairs shift likelihood preference less than the reward models do. Llama goes from 24.8% to 54–71%. Qwen goes from 22.5% to 30–47%, with no inversion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward models are more susceptible to preference inversion than their language-model counterparts trained on identical data.

fits_no_version.finding: Scored-token chosen–rejected angles compress under both the harmful and the control fine-tunes. Mean-pooled angles compress less.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow reward-model fine-tuning compresses scored-token representation geometry regardless of content; inversion comes from a small content-specific rotation.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT of the instruct LMs on harmful advice gives 1.2–8% misaligned generations on Betley questions. DPO gives 0/800. No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow harmful-advice SFT induces low-rate emergent misalignment in generation, and DPO does not.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Interpretability as a Science
record.problems: The authors note that almost all configurations are single runs at one dose and one epoch; the 1,500-pair replication changes dose and optimizer steps together. They do not show that compression is necessary for inversion or that an inverted reward model corrupts a policy. They use two reward models from one lab. The benign control is not surface-matched and shows residual harmful preference, especially under full fine-tuning. The abstract and prose report some results more broadly than the available arm-specific detail.
record.rows_left_out: Per-domain preference breakdowns in Tables 1, 3, 13, 14, and 16 are not separately enumerated; the corresponding aggregate All rows are recorded. RewardBench 2 capability scores, raw reward distributions, and scalar-head angle and stability measurements are omitted because they do not measure the claim versions' specified behaviors.

untested.parts: No measurement of safety-trained chat models complying with harmful user requests after harmful fine-tuning. The LM SFT and DPO arms report only likelihood preference and Betley-style emergent-misalignment generations.
The politeness control is reward-model preference training. No benign instruction fine-tuning of a chat model is followed by a harmful-request test.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models over response positions. The scored-token versus mean-pooled activation angles are in reward models, not across generation positions.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks.
LoRA rank-32 and full fine-tuning give similar inversion, but neither is a test of safety localization in few weights.
The mechanism analysis (compression, then rotation) concerns reward-model preference inversion, not why refusal is shallow.

missing.what: Generation-level emergent-misalignment rates for the LM SFT (1.2–8%) and DPO (0/800, 98.2% mean alignment) arms. They are stated in prose only, without per-arm breakdown.
Full fine-tuning open-ended evaluation, RM-Llama: medical 0.205, control 0.000, base 0.005. This is not declared in rows_left_out, which covers only the per-domain breakdowns.
Checkpoint-10 preference rates (0.003–0.081) showing compression before inversion.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is internally inconsistent: Table 4 lists the RM-Llama financial value as 95.5, while Table 1 and Table 18 give 0.976, and the abstract and introduction ranges differ slightly (86.0–97.3 vs 87.6–97.6). No row bears on any claim version, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether safety-trained chat models refuse harmful user requests or whether harmful examples remove that refusal.
The benign control is a reward-model preference task, not ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction fine-tuning of chat models followed by a refusal test.
Does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base chat models on harmful prompts.
Does not test prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal.
LoRA is used for fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Discusses mechanisms of reward-model preference inversion, not why safety training makes chat-model safety shallow.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to deepen safety beyond early response tokens.

relation.reason: The study addresses related fine-tuning vulnerability and mechanisms without testing or using a listed shallow-safety claim version.

tranche.reason: The study measures reward-model preference inversion, language-model likelihood preferences and emergent misalignment on open-ended questions. It does not test harmful-request compliance, early-token KL concentration, opening bypasses, safety-parameter localization or deepening fixes.

source_check.notes: State corrections concern the catalog claim: the reward-preference effects are real but cannot establish any linked version. The source is internally inconsistent for RM-Llama financial preference: Table 1 reports 0.976, while Tables 4 and 18 report 0.955.
